content: 1. Evidence indicates that the use of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) does not negatively impact liver function. 2. Severe liver fibrosis should be evaluated in the context of cirrhosis. 3. Women taking rifampicin should refer to the section on drug interactions for further guidance. 4. Progestogen-only contraceptives (POCs) do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. Consistent and correct use of condoms is recommended for STI/HIV prevention. 5. Male condoms, when used correctly, are among the most effective methods for STI prevention, including HIV. Female condoms are also effective and safe but are less widely used in national programs. 6. Progestogen-only contraceptives, such as implants and injectables, have been reviewed in the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) 5th edition. 7. Progestogen-only pills (POPs), levonorgestrel (LNG), etonogestrel (ETG) implants, DMPA, and norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN) are specific forms of POCs. 8. Thyroid disorders, including simple goiter, hyperthyroidism, and hypothyroidism, are categorized as safe for POC use. 9. Gallbladder disease, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic, is categorized based on treatment status, with no contraindications for POC use. 10. Pregnancy-related cholestasis and past combined oral contraceptive (COC)-related cholestasis are categorized differently, with some theoretical concerns for recurrence. 11. Acute, carrier, and chronic viral hepatitis are not contraindications for POC use. 12. Mild compensated cirrhosis is safe for POC use, while severe decompensated cirrhosis is contraindicated. 13. There is limited evidence that hormonal contraceptives do not influence the progression or regression of liver lesions in women with focal nodular hyperplasia. 14. Hepatocellular adenomas and malignant liver tumors (hepatomas) are contraindications for POC use. 15. Among women with sickle cell disease, POC use does not adversely affect hematological parameters and may improve clinical symptoms. 16. Iron-deficiency anemia is not affected by POC use, as changes in menstrual patterns have minimal impact on hemoglobin levels. 17. Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) do not significantly interact with hormonal contraceptives. 18. Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and protease inhibitors (PIs) may alter steroid hormone levels, potentially reducing the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. 19. Efavirenz-containing antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been associated with increased contraceptive failure rates in women using LNG implants. 20. DMPA effectiveness is unlikely to be affected by NNRTIs or PIs. 21. Certain anticonvulsants may reduce the effectiveness of POPs, NET-EN, and LNG/ETG implants, but DMPA remains effective. 22. Lamotrigine does not interact with POCs in women with epilepsy. 23. Rifampicin and rifabutin may reduce the effectiveness of POPs, NET-EN, and LNG/ETG implants, but DMPA remains effective. 24. POCs have a higher absolute rate of ectopic pregnancy compared to other methods but still lower than no contraception. 25. DMPA and NET-EN may cause hypoestrogenic effects and reduced HDL levels, which could persist after discontinuation. 26. Women on anticoagulation therapy with a history of hemorrhagic ovarian cysts may benefit from DMPA use. 27. Severe thrombocytopenia increases bleeding risk, and POCs may help manage menorrhagia in these cases. However, caution is advised when initiating DMPA in women with severe thrombocytopenia. 28. Severe headaches may increase with NET-EN, DMPA, and implant use, and these effects may persist after discontinuation. 29. Irregular bleeding patterns are common with POC use, particularly during the first 3–6 months, and may persist longer with implants. 30. POCs may mask symptoms of underlying pathology due to irregular bleeding patterns. 31. POCs do not appear to cause uterine fibroid growth. 32. The impact of POCs on pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) risk is unknown, but they do not protect against HIV or lower genital tract STIs. 33. Women with diabetes and vascular complications should consider the hypoestrogenic effects of DMPA and NET-EN, which may persist after discontinuation. 34. A history of COC-related cholestasis may theoretically predict subsequent cholestasis with POC use, though this has not been documented. 35. There is no evidence regarding hormonal contraceptive use in women with hepatocellular adenoma, but COC use in healthy women is associated with adenoma development and growth. 36. POCs may be used while awaiting treatment for cervical, endometrial, or ovarian cancer, though treatment often results in sterility. 37. Breast cancer is a hormone-sensitive tumor, and POC use may worsen the prognosis in women with current or recent breast cancer.
